name: Illusory correlation
statement: People report an association between two things that were paired no more often than chance allows, most readily when both of them are rare.
meaning: Two separate research programmes share the name. The first is about clinical judgement. Loren and Jean Chapman showed that psychologists reading projective test protocols report sign-symptom pairings that are not in the data, and that undergraduates shown rigged materials rediscover the same pairings. The second is about stereotype formation. Hamilton and Gifford gave people statements about two invented groups, kept the ratio of desirable to undesirable behaviour identical for both, and made one group and one behaviour type rarer than the other. Participants then judged the smaller group more harshly. Because the smaller group and the rarer behaviour are both distinctive, their co-occurrence is said to be over-recorded, which supplies a route to a negative stereotype with no hostility behind it. The two literatures test different claims with different materials, and a result in one carries no weight in the other. The clustering illusion is entry 60, apophenia entry 41 and the Texas sharpshooter fallacy entry 52; each concerns pattern in a single stream of events rather than covariation between two.

origin.who: Loren J. Chapman and Jean P. Chapman
origin.note: "Genesis of popular but erroneous psychodiagnostic observations" reports six studies in which undergraduates viewed Draw-a-Person drawings paired at random with symptom statements. Loren Chapman published a single-author word-pair study under the same name in the Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior four months earlier. Mullen and Johnson treat that paper as the original demonstration, and write that subjects consistently overestimated how often the two longest words in the list had been paired together. Neither 1967 paper was obtained; both are cited here from the descriptions given by Watts, Smith and Lilienfeld and by Mullen and Johnson.

evidence: The clinical findings are quoted here at one remove. Watts, Smith and Lilienfeld report that in the Chapmans' survey 91% of clinicians said atypical eyes on the Draw-a-Person test indicate suspiciousness, and 82% said a large or emphasised head indicates intelligence. In the experiment that followed, drawings were paired with symptom statements so that each statement appeared once with each drawing, and undergraduates recovered the same pairings the clinicians named. The 1969 follow-up repeated the design with Rorschach protocols and signs of homosexuality, and the same account reports that undergraduates named the signs clinicians named, with actual correlations of zero in the materials. The minority-group paradigm is documented in Mullen and Johnson's meta-analytic table. Hamilton and Gifford's Experiment 1 used 39 statements split 18 desirable and 8 undesirable for the majority against 9 and 4 for the minority, with 33 participants, and gave t(32) = 2.57 on the assignment measure and t(32) = 1.92 on estimation. Their Experiment 2 made desirable behaviour the rare kind, used a 36-statement array with cells of 16, 8, 8 and 4 and 52 participants, and gave t(51) = 3.04 and t(51) = 1.75. Hamilton repeated the paradigm himself with Dugan and Trolier in 1985, and the same table records estimation tests of t(39) = 2.46 on 40 people and t(23) = 2.98 on 24. Mullen and Johnson pooled 14 articles reporting 23 studies. Across 28 estimation tests the combined effect was r = 0.344, and across 23 assignment tests r = 0.259, which they call moderate and small-to-moderate. Their diffuse comparisons of significance levels gave chi-square 53.208 on 27 degrees of freedom and 46.222 on 22, and they describe both sets as significantly heterogeneous. The valence of the rare behaviour separated the studies sharply. Where it was negative the pooled effects were r = 0.460 over 17 tests and r = 0.385 over 13; where it was not, r = 0.213 over 11 and r = 0.156 over 10, and the focused comparisons gave z = 3.436, p = .00030 and z = 2.984, p = .00142. Mullen and Johnson note that the studies which had varied valence directly, Hamilton and Gifford among them, had suggested it makes little or no difference, and they present their own result as the first demonstration of the pattern.

examples.tag: The small team and the rare mistake
examples.text: One department of four people and one of forty make errors at the same rate. The few errors in the small team are doubly unusual, are noticed together, and the team acquires a reputation the rates do not contain.

examples.tag: The sign a marker is sure about
examples.text: An examiner becomes convinced that candidates who write in very large hand are the anxious ones. The pairing occurs no more often than chance allows, and the conviction survives because the striking cases are the ones recalled.

examples.tag: The newcomers in a small town
examples.text: Newcomers are a tenth of a town's residents and account for a tenth of its offences. Both the group and the offences are uncommon, so the pairs stand out, and residents report a link the rate does not hold.

replication.headline: Four preregistered experiments, each analysing between 1,395 and 1,551 people, found the effect on self-reported evaluation whenever the rare behaviour was undesirable, at d = 0.20 to 0.33, and none of it on three implicit measures.
replication.detail: Van Dessel, Ratliff, Brannon, Gawronski and De Houwer ran four preregistered experiments through the Project Implicit website. They recruited 3,557, 3,825, 3,334 and 3,675 volunteers and analysed 1,535, 1,432, 1,395 and 1,551. Each used the standard array of 16 and 8 statements for the majority against 8 and 4 for the minority. On self-reported evaluation the classic effect appeared in all four when positive statements were the frequent kind, so that the rare behaviour was the undesirable one: d = 0.28 with a Bayes factor of 170.54, d = 0.20 with 11.50, d = 0.23 with 8.92, and d = 0.33 with a Bayes factor above 1,000. When negative statements were the frequent kind the picture broke up. Experiments 2 and 3 gave the mirror effect, the minority preferred, at d = 0.18, p = .015, Bayes factor 2.32, and at d = 0.24, Bayes factor 12.76. Experiments 1 and 4 gave nothing, at d = 0.11 with a Bayes factor of 0.70 and d = 0.10 with 0.55. The authors summarise the whole set as a preference for the majority when more statements were positive and a preference for the minority when more were negative. No illusory correlation appeared on any implicit measure. The crucial interaction gave F(1, 1527) = 0.26, p = .61, Bayes factor 0.08 on the Implicit Association Test, F(1, 1254) = 0.72, p = .40, Bayes factor 0.13 on the Affect Misattribution Procedure, and F(1, 1542) = 0.86, p = .36, Bayes factor 0.12 on the Evaluative Priming Task. Failures predate this. Mullen and Johnson's table records seven hypothesis tests from Feldman, Camburn and Gatti's four experiments, including an estimation test of r = -0.272 running the wrong way, and Mullen and Johnson describe those four studies as having consistently failed to provide compelling support for the effect. Murphy, Schmeer, Vallee-Tourangeau, Mondragon and Hilton report, in an abstract read at PubMed, that the effect was initially absent, emerged with intermediate amounts of experience, and was eliminated with increased experience. Fiedler's information-loss account holds that no distinctiveness mechanism is needed, only regressive judgement from a smaller sample of minority information. Weigl, Mecklinger and Rosburg read that account as predicting no effect when positive and negative behaviours are equally frequent, and their simulation of Fiedler's BIAS model over 1,000 runs bore the prediction out: illusory correlation at noise levels one to four with skewed frequencies, all t > 21.03, and nothing with equated frequencies, all absolute t(999) < 1.06, p > .289. Their participants did not co-operate. With skewed frequencies and 28 analysed people the effect appeared on all three measures, at F(1, 27) = 14.93 for assignment, 4.59 for estimation and 10.30 for evaluation. With equated frequencies and 30 people it appeared on all three again, at F(1, 29) = 9.53, 6.26 and 6.71, and the illusory-correlation coefficients did not differ between the two experiments, all F < 1, p > .635. The clinical paradigm has also been re-run. Kurtz and Garfield used Chapman and Chapman's own 1969 materials, added a simulated training session, and found training no more effective than no training at reducing the effect, which they report as consistent with Chapman and Chapman.

study.cite: Van Dessel, P., Ratliff, K., Brannon, S. M., Gawronski, B., & De Houwer, J. (2021). Illusory-Correlation Effects on Implicit and Explicit Evaluation. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 47(10), 1480-1494.

limits: Hamilton and Gifford's own report was not obtained, so no figure on this page comes from it. The correlations usually quoted for it, r = 0.414 and r = 0.321 for the two measures of Experiment 1, are Mullen and Johnson's conversions of the t values in their table rather than figures Hamilton and Gifford printed. The Chapmans' two papers were not obtained either, and every clinical figure here comes from an encyclopedia entry by Watts, Smith and Lilienfeld. Fiedler's 1991 paper was not obtained, and the account is described through Weigl and colleagues, who implemented its model. The structured effect size is one condition of one of four preregistered experiments, and it is not a summary of the literature. Mullen and Johnson's pooled figures carry no publication-bias test beyond fail-safe numbers, 1,964.5 for estimation and 790.7 for assignment, which say how many null studies would have to be missing rather than whether any are. Four of the seven Feldman, Camburn and Gatti tests in their table are reconstructions entered at p = .50 rather than statistics those authors reported. Weigl and colleagues analysed 28 of 34 people in one experiment and 30 in the other. No statistics are quoted here from Murphy and colleagues, whose full text was not obtained.
misreadings: The clinical result and the minority-group result are routinely cited as one finding. They share a name and a first author and nothing else. One is about experts reading projective tests, the other about undergraduates reading sentences about invented groups, and the replication record for the second says nothing about the first. The second common error is to read the paradigm as showing that people dislike minorities. What it tracks is the rare behaviour, and when the rare behaviour is desirable the effect weakens or turns round. Mullen and Johnson pooled r = 0.213 and r = 0.156 for non-negative rare behaviour against 0.460 and 0.385 for negative, and Van Dessel and colleagues found the minority preferred in two of their four tests of the reversed arrangement. A third error treats the effect as a fixed property of the mind. It is a property of a particular stimulus array, it goes away with more training, and it does not appear on measures that give people no time to guess. Distinctiveness is also still contested as the mechanism. Weigl and colleagues found source memory better for the majority than the minority for both positive items, t(57) = 17.04, and negative items, t(57) = 10.81, which is the reverse of what a shared-distinctiveness account predicts, and no heightened retrieval accuracy for negative descriptions of the minority in the group assignment task. They do record one crumb for the account, negative items remembered better than positive ones for the minority at the immediate test, and they call it tentative at t(57) = -1.70, p = .095.

sources.text: Chapman, L. J., & Chapman, J. P. (1967). Genesis of popular but erroneous psychodiagnostic observations. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 72(3), 193-204. Not obtained on 21 September 2026: closed at the APA, no open copy at Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, Internet Archive or the web, and no abstract in the PubMed record. The PsycNET record, which does carry an abstract, is behind a bot challenge rather than a paywall. Cited through Watts, Smith and Lilienfeld.

Chapman, L. J., & Chapman, J. P. (1969). Illusory correlation as an obstacle to the use of valid psychodiagnostic signs. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 74(3), 271-280. Not obtained on 21 September 2026, by the same route and with the same result as the 1967 paper. Cited through Watts, Smith and Lilienfeld.

Chapman, L. J. (1967). Illusory correlation in observational report. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 6(1), 151-155. Not obtained on 21 September 2026; closed at Elsevier and no open copy located. Described here as Mullen and Johnson describe it.

Watts, A. L., Smith, S. F., & Lilienfeld, S. O. (2015). Illusory Correlation. In R. L. Cautin & S. O. Lilienfeld (Eds.), The Encyclopedia of Clinical Psychology, 1-8. Wiley. Full text read from the copy on Lilienfeld's own site; the source for the 91% and 82% survey figures and for the description of both Chapman studies.

Hamilton, D. L., & Gifford, R. K. (1976). Illusory correlation in interpersonal perception: A cognitive basis of stereotypic judgments. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 12(4), 392-407. Not obtained on 21 September 2026; closed at Elsevier, with no open copy at Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar or the web. The design and statistics on this page are read off Mullen and Johnson's Table 1 and Figure 1.

Mullen, B., & Johnson, C. (1990). Distinctiveness-based illusory correlations and stereotyping: A meta-analytic integration. British Journal of Social Psychology, 29(1), 11-28. Full text read; the pooled effects, the valence comparison, the fail-safe numbers and the per-study table are theirs.

Hamilton, D. L., Dugan, P. M., & Trolier, T. K. (1985). The formation of stereotypic beliefs: Further evidence for distinctiveness-based illusory correlations. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 48(1), 5-17. Not obtained; the two estimation tests quoted here are read off Mullen and Johnson's Table 1.

Feldman, J. M., Camburn, A., & Gatti, G. M. (1986). Shared distinctiveness as a source of illusory correlation in performance appraisal. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 37(1), 34-59. Not obtained; the seven hypothesis tests quoted here are read off Mullen and Johnson's Table 1.

Fiedler, K. (1991). The tricky nature of skewed frequency tables: An information loss account of distinctiveness-based illusory correlations. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 60(1), 24-36. Not obtained on 21 September 2026: closed at the APA, nothing at Unpaywall or Semantic Scholar, and no copy on the author's Heidelberg pages that a web search could reach. The account is described here as Weigl, Mecklinger and Rosburg describe and implement it.

Van Dessel, P., Ratliff, K., Brannon, S. M., Gawronski, B., & De Houwer, J. (2021). Illusory-Correlation Effects on Implicit and Explicit Evaluation. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 47(10), 1480-1494. Full text of the published article read from the copy on Gawronski's site; four preregistered experiments.

Weigl, M., Mecklinger, A., & Rosburg, T. (2018). Illusory correlations despite equated category frequencies: A test of the information loss account. Consciousness and Cognition, 63, 11-28. Full text of the published article read from the copy on the Saarland University page; the BIAS simulation and both experiments.

Kurtz, R. M., & Garfield, S. L. (1978). Illusory correlation: A further exploration of Chapman's paradigm. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 46(5), 1009-1015. Full text not obtained; read as the abstract in the ERIC record EJ221053, which states that the materials were Chapman and Chapman's 1969 ones and that training did not reduce the effect. PubMed carries no abstract for it.

Dowling, J. F., & Graham, J. R. (1976). Illusory correlation and the MMPI. Journal of Personality Assessment, 40(5), 531-538. Read as the PubMed abstract; 28 naive and 26 experienced student judges both produced large amounts of illusory correlation, the experienced judges more.

Murphy, R. A., Schmeer, S., Vallee-Tourangeau, F., Mondragon, E., & Hilton, D. (2011). Making the illusory correlation effect appear and then disappear: The effects of increased learning. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(1), 24-40. Read as the PubMed abstract; no statistics are quoted here.

Eder, A. B., Fiedler, K., & Hamm-Eder, S. (2011). Illusory correlations revisited: The role of pseudocontingencies and working-memory capacity. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(3), 517-532. Read as the PubMed abstract; reports the bias growing as working-memory capacity falls.
